title: The new 900-seat Club Plantation and Leonard Reed's show
summary: Back in St. Louis they open a larger club, Pillars scolds the head waiter, Leonard Reed produces the show, and the owners decline to hire Lena Horne.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Did you come back to the Plantation here in St. Louis?

Oh, yes. The place burned, so we all got together and we all came on back to St. Louis. And we opened up a new club here, a bigger place, where they could absorb all of the people, see. They was turning away enough money on the weekend to pay the net for a week.
So this was a new club, like.
This was a new Club Plantation, much larger place. It could seat around about 900 people, see.

And then one night, we came to work, they had them up on each side of the bandstand. I told the head waiter, I said, Look here, don't you never do this no more, you know what I mean. Now, you run the dining room but you don't run the bandstand, you know what I mean. He had to be told, you know what I mean? Putting people up on the bandstand like that. You know, the head waiter was the type of guy that if you showed him a five dollar bill, man, -- . He made a lot of money.
That's when we had Leonard Reed.
Yeah, Leonard Reed opened the show. He opened the show. Leonard Reed opened the show with us.
We opened up here -- that was the year we had Skins on drums, that was the year that George Hudson left the band.

And that was the year Lena Horne came through here, and the owners of the club could have hired her for a couple hundred dollars a week. And they said, 'No, no, too much money.' So Lena left and went on to California. And she hasn't looked back since. That actually happened. 1940.
